source: The four whales slain that evening had died wide apart; one, far to windward; one, less distant, to leeward; one ahead; one astern. These last three were brought alongside ere nightfall; but the windward one could not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay by its side all night; and that boat was Ahab’s.

The waif-pole was thrust upright into the dead whale’s spout-hole; and the lantern hanging from its top, cast a troubled flickering glare upon the black, glossy back, and far out upon the midnight waves, which gently chafed the whale’s broad flank, like soft surf upon a beach.

Ahab and all his boat’s crew seemed asleep but the Parsee; who crouching in the bow, sat watching the sharks, that spectrally played round the whale, and tapped the light cedar planks with their tails. A sound like the moaning in squadrons over Asphaltites of unforgiven ghosts of Gomorrah, ran shuddering through the air.
Started from his slumbers, Ahab, face to face, saw the Parsee; and hooped round by the gloom of the night they seemed the last men in a flooded world. “I have dreamed it again,” said he.
“Of the hearses? Have I not said, old man, that neither hearse nor coffin can be thine?”
“And who are hearsed that die on the sea?”

“But I said, old man, that ere thou couldst die on this voyage, two hearses must verily be seen by thee on the sea; the first not made by mortal hands; and the visible wood of the last one must be grown in America.”
“Aye, aye! a strange sight that, Parsee:—a hearse and its plumes floating over the ocean with the waves for the pall-bearers. Ha! Such a sight we shall not soon see.”
“Believe it or not, thou canst not die till it be seen, old man.”
“And what was that saying about thyself?”
“Though it come to the last, I shall still go before thee thy pilot.”

“And when thou art so gone before—if that ever befall—then ere I can follow, thou must still appear to me, to pilot me still?—Was it not so? Well, then, did I believe all ye say, oh my pilot! I have here two pledges that I shall yet slay Moby Dick and survive it.”
“Take another pledge, old man,” said the Parsee, as his eyes lighted up like fire-flies in the gloom—“Hemp only can kill thee.”
“The gallows, ye mean.—I am immortal then, on land and on sea,” cried Ahab, with a laugh of derision;—“Immortal on land and on sea!”
Both were silent again, as one man. The grey dawn came on, and the slumbering crew arose from the boat’s bottom, and ere noon the dead whale was brought to the ship.

modern_en.title: Chapter 117 — The Whale Watch
paragraphs: The four whales killed that evening had died wide apart; one far to windward, one less distant to leeward, one ahead, one astern. These last three were brought alongside before nightfall; but the windward one could not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay by its side all night. And that boat was Ahab's.

The waif-pole, the pole planted to mark a dead whale, was thrust upright into the dead whale's spout-hole; and the lantern hanging from its top cast a troubled flickering glare upon the black, glossy back, and far out upon the midnight waves, which gently chafed the whale's broad flank, like soft surf upon a beach.

Ahab and all his boat's crew seemed asleep but the Parsee; who, crouching in the bow, sat watching the sharks that spectrally played round the whale and tapped the light cedar planks with their tails. A sound like the moaning of unforgiven ghosts of Gomorrah, in squadrons over Asphaltites (the Dead Sea), ran shuddering through the air.

Starting from his slumbers, Ahab found himself face to face with the Parsee; and hooped round by the gloom of the night, they seemed the last men in a flooded world. "I have dreamed it again," he said.
"The hearses? Haven't I told you, old man, that you can have neither hearse nor coffin?"
"And who that dies on the sea is ever hearsed?"

"But I said, old man, that before you could die on this voyage, two hearses must truly be seen by you on the sea; the first not made by mortal hands; and the visible wood of the last one must be grown in America."
"Aye, aye! A strange sight that, Parsee: a hearse and its plumes floating over the ocean with the waves for the pallbearers. Ha! Such a sight we shall not soon see."
"Believe it or not, you cannot die until it is seen, old man."
"And what was that saying about yourself?"
"Even if it comes to the last, I shall still go before you, your pilot."

"And when you are so gone before — if that ever happens — then before I can follow, you must still appear to me, to pilot me still? Was it not so? Well, then, if I believed all you say, oh my pilot, I have here two pledges that I shall yet slay Moby Dick and survive it."
"Take another pledge, old man," said the Parsee, as his eyes lit up like fireflies in the gloom — "Hemp only can kill you."
"The gallows, you mean. I am immortal then, on land and on sea," cried Ahab, with a laugh of derision. "Immortal on land and on sea!"
Once more both fell silent, as if they were one man. The gray dawn came, the sleeping crew got up from the bottom of the boat, and before noon the dead whale had been brought to the ship.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 117 — Hvalvagten
paragraphs: De fire hvaler, der blev dræbt den aften, var døde langt fra hinanden; en langt til luvart, en mindre langt væk til læ, en forude, en agterude. De sidste tre blev bragt langs siden før nattens frembrud; men den på luvsiden kunne ikke nås før om morgenen; og båden, der havde dræbt den, lå ved dens side hele natten. Og den båd var Ahabs.

Hvalstangen, stangen, der plantes for at markere en død hval, var stukket lodret ned i den døde hvals blæsehul; og lanternen, der hang fra dens top, kastede et uroligt, flakkende skær over den sorte, blanke ryg og langt ud over midnatsbølgerne, som blidt gnavede mod hvalens brede flanke, som blød brænding mod en strand.

Ahab og hele hans bådsmandskab syntes at sove, undtagen parsien, som sad sammenkrøbet i stævnen og iagttog hajerne, der spøgelsesagtigt legede rundt om hvalen og bankede på de lette cedertræsplanker med deres haler. En lyd som jamren fra Gomorras utilgivne genfærd, i eskadroner over Asfaltsøen (Det Døde Hav), løb gysende gennem luften.
Ahab for op af sin søvn og fandt sig ansigt til ansigt med parsien; og indhyllet i nattens mørke så de ud som de sidste mænd i en oversvømmet verden. »Jeg har drømt det igen,« sagde han.
»Ligvognene? Har jeg ikke sagt dig, gamle mand, at du hverken kan få ligvogn eller kiste?«
»Og hvem, der dør på havet, bliver nogensinde kørt i ligvogn?«

»Men jeg sagde, gamle mand, at før De kan dø på denne rejse, må De med egne øjne se to ligvogne på havet. Den første er ikke lavet af menneskehænder, og træet i den sidste, som kan ses, skal være vokset i Amerika.«
»Ja, ja! Et mærkeligt syn, parsi: en ligvogn med sine fjerbuske, der flyder hen over havet med bølgerne som ligbærere. Ha! Det syn får vi ikke så snart at se.«
»Tro det eller lad være, gamle mand, De kan ikke dø, før det er set.«
»Og hvad var det, du sagde om dig selv?«
»Selv om det kommer til det sidste, vil jeg stadig gå forud for Dem, Deres lods.«

»Og når du er gået forud på den måde — hvis det nogensinde sker — så skal du alligevel vise dig for mig, før jeg kan følge efter, for at lodse mig endnu? Var det ikke sådan? Nå, så hvis jeg troede på alt, hvad du siger, o min lods, så har jeg her to løfter om, at jeg endnu skal dræbe Moby Dick og overleve det.«
»Tag endnu et løfte, gamle mand,« sagde parsien, mens hans øjne lyste op som ildfluer i mørket — »Kun hamp kan dræbe Dem.«
»Galgen, mener du. Så er jeg altså udødelig, både på land og til søs,« råbte Ahab med en hånlig latter. »Udødelig på land og til søs!«
Endnu en gang faldt begge i tavshed, som om de var én mand. Den grå dagning kom, den sovende besætning rejste sig fra bunden af båden, og før middag var den døde hval bragt hen til skibet.
